director.chapterArc: A hard number unsettles Callie, then competence and dry companionship establish the caravan’s working rhythm. The hunter-line forces a disciplined concealment and exposes the practical limits of power. In the night, inherited mythology is stripped down to an indifferent fact: the door opens, or it does not. The chapter then turns from abstract uncertainty to undeniable bodily decline as Callie’s mother loses control of her leg, hand, and awareness. Wordless care replaces denial. Katori quietly rearranges the wagon to make room, lets one private name escape, and converts Pell’s grim estimate into a decision to leave early.
director.restraintNote: Keep Calder grounded and observant. Let arithmetic, physical failures, and practical accommodations carry the emotion; never announce Callie’s grief. The Ember and door material must sound ordinary and factual, not mystical. Humor is dry self-protection, fear remains tactically articulate, and the final acts of care should register without sentimentality. Restore the full Original Calder baseline after every cue.

cues.delivery: Pell prices the journey like worn equipment: dry, exact, and faintly amused by the inevitability of additional failure.
cues.from: "It's not wrong, it's just not yours." Pell had the atlas open on the board beside him with the pencil laid in the crease, and he did not look up from the mules. "Yours is fifteen and yours is a girl and a barrow doing eleven miles a day and never stopping for anything, and I don't doubt it for a second. Mine is nine hundred pounds of freight on a wagon with one spare wheel. Nineteen days. That's if the causeway's standing where you say it's standing, and if neither of these two goes lame on me, and if it doesn't rain the way it rained on us in the Warren." He clicked his tongue at the mule. "Three ifs. I price an if at a day. Call it twenty-two and be happy with me if I'm wrong."

cues.delivery: Let the arithmetic slow as Callie reaches the cost she has avoided; keep it analytical until the final exchange becomes unbearable by implication alone.
cues.from: She was doing the other arithmetic, the one she had been refusing to do since yesterday morning, and it came out the same however she started it. Four days. Four days more than she'd have made alone, and on the other side of the ledger her mother was lying on the boards behind her with her arm across her eyes instead of walking eleven miles on a leg that had started doing a thing Callie did not have a name for.
cues.through: Four days of the road, bought with four days of her mother.
cues.reason: The travel estimate becomes a calculation of her mother’s remaining life.

cues.delivery: Keep Callie’s tactical answer precise despite the dry mouth; the fear is that other lives now depend on her judgment, not that danger is nearby.
cues.from: "Not the verge," she said. "The verge is where they lie up when they stop. Road bed's flat and open and we'd be a shape on it. There's a stand of scrub willow about two hundred paces back on the south side with a dry gully behind it. It's low and it's downwind and there's one way in." She swallowed. "And nobody makes any noise, and nobody makes a fire, and — "

cues.delivery: State the rule firmly, with only a slight disturbance at hearing inherited knowledge become Callie’s own authority.
cues.from: "Because they come at worked power." Callie heard her own voice come out flat and certain and slightly frightened of itself. "That's — everybody knows that. A man at Gaunt's Reach told me a lit-up man on a road at night is the brightest thing in this country and everything that hunts comes at it, and I don't know if that's true, but he was the kind of man who'd have been there."

cues.reason: Callie risks contradicting Katori and discovers that her warning is correct.

cues.delivery: Hold the stillness taut and spatially clear. Do not accelerate; each distant sound matters because nobody can safely react to it.
cues.from: Nothing came. That was the whole event and Callie knew it was the whole event by the second hour and still could not make her shoulders come down. Twice something went through the scrub off to the north-east, unhurried, not near. Once there was a long dry sound like somebody prying a board off a nail, very far away, and Otto's hand went around the wagon pole and stayed there, and Ines said "Eight hundred," to nobody, and the sound did not come again.

cues.delivery: A genuinely hushed question, released only when prolonged vigilance makes silence briefly harder to bear.
cues.from: "How many have you got?" Callie whispered, eventually.
cues.through: "How many have you got?" Callie whispered, eventually.
cues.reason: The manuscript explicitly places the exchange inside concealment.

cues.delivery: Ines inventories disappointment without self-pity. Keep the tragedy correction flat; let the years of waiting and other people’s judgment supply the ache.
cues.from: "It opened onto nothing," said Ines. "I sat in my mother's kitchen and they said the words over me and nothing happened, and I waited two years to see if it was slow, and it wasn't slow, it was nothing." Left to right, and back. "I'm thirty-one and I can put an arrow into a hound at ninety paces in bad light. You can decide for yourself how much of a tragedy that is. Most people decide for me."

cues.reason: Her failed opening reframes power and worth.

cues.delivery: Katori teaches an ordinary mechanism, not a mystery. Allow one buried personal cost to surface only at the unwanted final shape, then contain it.
cues.from: "That's not a threat and it's not a warning," Katori said. "It's the actual answer and it's the one nobody gives you, so listen. Mine happened in a room with eleven of my own family in it and somebody's grandmother saying words over the top of my head. I was thirteen and four months. I sat down and I stood up and the only thing that was different about me was that everybody in the room had decided to look at me for an hour." She shifted on the tailgate. "It's a door. One door. It opens somewhere behind you and you can't see it and mostly you can't feel it, and it's about as dramatic as a lamp being lit in a house on the other side of a hill. And then it's nine months before your Ember so much as gets warm, and then it's eleven years, and at the end of the eleven years you have one shape, and the shape is not the one you wanted."

cues.reason: The explanation carries both reassurance and the quiet loss of imagined possibility.

cues.delivery: Callie admits the feared omission reluctantly; keep the broken sentence small and private, as though saying it might make the defect real.
cues.from: "There weren't any words said over me," she said. "There wasn't anybody left in Thistle Ford to say them and my mother couldn't — " She stopped. "There weren't any words."
cues.through: "There weren't any words said over me," she said. "There wasn't anybody left in Thistle Ford to say them and my mother couldn't — " She stopped. "There weren't any words."
cues.reason: Her abstract anxiety becomes a personal confession.

cues.delivery: Pell dismantles ceremony with sleepy historical bluntness. Land the absurdity dryly, then make the final order practical reassurance rather than ridicule.
cues.from: "I'm sixty-one," Pell said, to the underside of the wagon. "The whole business is about as old as I am. When it came for me there was nobody to say anything over me because nobody had thought of anything to say yet — we were all thirteen and none of our parents had ever heard of it and half the country thought we'd caught something. The words came later. Somebody's grandmother invented them about thirty-five years ago and now people say them slowly and think they're old." He rolled over. "The words are for the people in the room. The door does what it does. It has never once in sixty years asked anybody's permission and it is not going to start with you. Go to sleep."

cues.delivery: A quick defensive joke from a woman trying to preserve ordinary authority; keep the wit intact but let its new fragility show underneath.
cues.from: "Then I've been thinking it very loudly."
cues.through: "Then I've been thinking it very loudly."
cues.reason: This is the mother’s last successful comic deflection before the decline becomes undeniable.

cues.delivery: Otto makes help impersonal and logistical so she can accept it without humiliation. Warmth stays entirely inside the efficiency.
cues.from: And then Otto was there, and he did not ask, and he did not make any kind of face about it, he simply crouched and got an arm under her and stood up with her the way he had stood up with the barrow, and said, "There's a crate digging in, I'll shift it," and carried her to the wagon.

cues.reason: His tact changes the social meaning of being carried.

cues.delivery: Give the acceptance more weight than the fall. Stay inside Callie’s observation, with no overt mourning; the cold arrives when resistance does not.
cues.through: That was the thing. Callie stood in the road with her hook in her hand and watched her mother be carried eleven paces by a boy she had known for nine days, and not fight it, and not say one single funny thing about it, and that was the moment the cold got all the way into her.
cues.reason: Callie recognizes the severity of her mother’s decline.

cues.delivery: Render the repeated failed braiding patiently and without pity. The hidden hour and refusal to react are the emotional facts.
cues.from: She was trying with both hands and her right hand was not doing what she was telling it to. She would get two passes and the right hand would let go of its strand, and she would start again, and get two passes, and the right hand would let go. She did it four times while Callie stood there. She was not crying and she was not swearing. She was working at it with enormous patience, in the dark, at three in the morning, where nobody would see her fail at it.

cues.reason: Physical repetition exposes the mother’s private loss of control.

cues.delivery: Concentrate all tenderness into the hard grip and its brief duration; both women end contact before it can become acknowledgment.
cues.from: Her mother put her hand back and found Callie's wrist and held it, hard, for about three seconds, which was as long as either of them could stand.
cues.through: Her mother put her hand back and found Callie's wrist and held it, hard, for about three seconds, which was as long as either of them could stand.
cues.reason: Their restraint makes the touch the chapter’s clearest mutual admission.

cues.delivery: Keep the endearment ordinary, then let Callie—not the mother—register the missed substitution. No vocal break; the blankness is more damaging.
cues.from: "Thank you, love," her mother said, and drank, and did not notice, and there was nothing at all in her face to show that anything had gone past her.
cues.through: "Thank you, love," her mother said, and drank, and did not notice, and there was nothing at all in her face to show that anything had gone past her.
cues.reason: Cognitive decline lands beneath an unchanged domestic gesture.

cues.delivery: The name escapes below intended hearing, private and indistinct. Do not shape it as a revelation or invite the listener to decipher it.
cues.from: When Katori finished she stood for a moment with her hands on the tailgate, looking at nothing, with her head down. And she said a name.

cues.reason: Katori’s concealed personal motive briefly breaches her control.
